newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pledges greater free trade efforts for Latam.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pledges greater free trade efforts for Latam.

text.p: The U.S. government, responding to charges of foot-dragging from Latin American and Caribbean leaders, pledged on Monday to renew its efforts to spread free trade throughout the Americas.

President Bill Clinton, who begins a visit to Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean May 5, "is determined to regain the momentum we all felt at the Summit of the Americas" in December 1994, Thomas "Mack" McClarty, Clinton's special envoy to the Americas, said in a speech.
"If we stand still we will only lose ground."
He was taking part in a two-day forum organised by former U.S. President Jimmy Carter to hammer out a common agenda for the Western hemisphere in the 21st century.

Latin American and Caribbean leaders charged earlier Monday that since the 1994 Miami summit, where 34 regional governments pledged to create a free trade area from the Yukon to Tierra del Fuego by 2005, little had been achieved and much impetus lost.
Bolivian President Gustavo Sanchez de Lozada said "a bucket of cold water" had fallen on the United States' free trade efforts in Latin America.

Republican opposition leader Newt Gingrich, the Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives, also pledged his support, saying in a speech: "I am dedicated deeply to passing 'fast track' legislation this year" and promising to include the Caribbean in any such free trade measure.

"Fast track" legislation would give any new trade pact Congressional treatment similar to that afforded the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) with Mexico and Canada, which was voted on as a whole and not opened up to debate about provisions for specific industries or sectors.
Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo said NAFTA had been a success for all three countries involved and called for greater economic openness in the hemisphere.
He added his voice, though, to those of fellow Latin American and Caribbean leaders who accused the United States of arrogance in its war on drugs.

"Claiming that other countries are the problem does not stop a single illegal transaction or save a single life," Zedillo said, adding that antinarcotics cooperation must be "totally respectful of every nation's sovereignty."

Jamaica Prime Minister P.J. Patterson criticized the controversial "certification" process by which the United States annually announces which other countries continue to be allies in its anti-narcotics efforts.
"Certification ... does not make for partnership, it does not make for friendship ... it is obvious that the process does more harm than good," Patterson said.

Organization of American States Secretary General Cesar Gaviria, a former president of Colombia, also weighed in, telling delegates "certification is unilateral" and something to be avoided in the future.
Latin American nations resent the process, which they consider an insult to their antinarcotics efforts.
U.S. drug czar Gen. Barry McCaffrey barely disagreed.

"Many would argue that we need clearly to establish a more multinational and cooperative relationship if we expect to make any progress on this terrible issue," he said, adding that the U.S. Congress should look again at the law requiring certification.
Gingrich said certification in its current form "doesn't make sense" and was "offensive" to other countries.
U.S. Vice President Al Gore was scheduled to speak at the forum's closing dinner on Tuesday.
